results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 67 body units' outline summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01..p67, with p59, p60 before p58 as the spec orders them). The three introduction callouts match no spec paragraph and are correctly unmatched; they hold the thesis statement and roadmap the spec places there.

Two units were marked two_ideas. Tax, Markets and Currencies ¶5 (converted vs fixed prices / rounding): the spec's p22 controlling idea joins both (choose a policy, and rounding matters because prices are compared to the cent), so it is one idea with its consequence. In Practice ¶4 (platform lists suffice / April 2027 ownership): the first sentence closes the test of the first assumption and is the declared transition into p48 (carries over 'what the vendors document about the first assumption'); the paragraph's controlling idea is the ownership agreement. Its wording is convoluted, which is recorded under flow_is_followable.

Every body unit serves a supporting claim through its section: scene S4; made-of S1/S2 (rule, moment, frozen price); tax S1/S3; eu-rules S3/S4 (history, channel rules as configuration); pieces S4 (engine vs copies, acknowledged/reconciled copies, authors); choices, trade-offs, stages S5; in-practice S1-S5 (limits, owners, events, daily comparison, frozen price, 30-day test, Price Drift at one day); goes-wrong S2/S3/S4. No orphan paragraphs.

Each evidence item is followed by what it shows: the Price Drift figures (410 x EUR 20 = EUR 8,200) and Figure 1; the dimension table ('a number selected from many by a rule'); commercetools/Adobe/SAP rules and the 'cheapest wins' vs 'most specific wins' reading; SAP KBA 2267117 and Adobe purchase orders ('correct for a negotiated order and wrong for a cart'); Directive 98/6/EC and Google Merchant Center; the VAT arithmetic (199/1.21 = 164.46, 199/1.19 = 167.23, 164.46 x 1.19 = 195.71, all correct) with 'a price stored without its tax basis is not' defensible; OSS; Shopify conversion; Article 6a and the ACM example (EUR 45.50 on EUR 50 = 9%, correct) followed by the history requirement; Amazon parity/price-control/PRICING_HEALTH followed by the architectural loop; the components and per-flow tables read in the next paragraphs; ChannelEngine guardrails; the trade-offs table read in its paragraph; the stage table and its judgement; Shopify/commercetools limits followed by 'the pattern'; Eva's table followed by the exchange; the Black Friday arithmetic (159/179 = 11%, 159/199 = 20%, window includes 27 Oct-3 Nov) with Figure 4.

Post level: both readers describe problem (the Price Drift) -> vocabulary in dependency order (price, rule, moment, tax, EU rules) -> components (engine vs copies, authors) -> choices, trade-offs, stages -> evidence (platform documentation, 2027 design, return to the Price Drift) -> failures -> synthesis, which agrees with the declared prerequisite_order with problem_solution, comparison and grouping. Neither reader found any section's position unclear; both say no section needs to move. Per section, every section is 'Clear' for both. The remaining lost-thread points are terms the declared audience already knows from Part I and product-information (failure-pattern names Long Fuse and Giant's Boots, Waypoint W5, iPaaS, EDI, idempotency, the scale-stage names including the trade-offs table's 'Omnichannel stage', Noor Visser and Eva, 'syndicated', bol) and the cities Nijmegen/Munich; they reflect the cold readers' not having read Part I, so they are not material for this audience. Reader A's note that the EDI failure lacks a Recovery line is a consistency remark, not a flow break; the spec (p60) declares detection only.

The introduction opens with the declared intriguing example (the Ridgewalker at EUR 199 for consumers and EUR 95 for wholesale), states the premise in ¶2 and the thesis in the KEY POINTS callout; no dictionary opening, throat-clearing or generic 'in today's world' pattern.

The conclusion does not merely restate or introduce new material: it reframes the opening's two prices, names what failed in the Price Drift, and joins the remedy and the legal duty in one dated record; the established / depends-on-context / author's-synthesis split and the questions apply it.

What to Take Away ¶1 gives the synthesis ('The remedy and the legal duty need the same record: a price kept once per kind, with the dates from which and until which it applies. That record ends a campaign without a restoring message, gives the daily comparison something to compare each copy against, and answers the 30-day question') and the so-what ('A merchant that keeps it can explain every price it shows, to a customer, a marketplace or a regulator'). The spec's contrasting half (one that types prices into each system finds out from a marketplace warning or a margin report) is left implicit; not a failure.

'The chapter opened with one jacket at €199 for a consumer and €95 for a wholesale buyer. Both prices are right, because each has a source and a rule that selects it. What went wrong in the Price Drift was not a price but a copy that nothing compared with its source.' This is the declared callback, answered as the spec says.

The intro reader predicted, in order: the Price Drift; what a price is made of and the selection rule; tax, markets and currencies; European rules; engine vs copies and who may change a price; four arrangements, trade-offs and scale stages; platform documentation and the 2027 design; how pricing fails. Evidence: the incident, EU consumer price rules, platform documentation, the 2027 design. This matches the expected sections and evidence. The reader's uncertainties (arrangements not named, stages undefined, whether 'who may change a price' is a separate section) concern detail the roadmap need not give.

The reader names the failed and unreported restore of EUR 199 ('the update restoring €199 failed. The ERP connector logged an error but reported success'), the daily reconciliation of every copy against its source as what catches it the next morning, and the 2027 campaign as one row with a start and an end so no restore message is needed. Does not propose pushing more often. Matches expected. (The reader's worry about 'the morning of 5 October' is not an inconsistency: under the 2027 design the campaign row ends on 4 October.)

The reader answers that the price is selected once at order placement, so the post-campaign list price is charged, frozen on the order, and the invoice copies it and never selects again, quoting 'The invoice never selects; it copies.' Matches expected. The reader notes that 'a cart holds it' (What a Price Is Made Of ¶5) could be misread as the cart locking the price; the rest of the chapter rules this out.

The reader answers that the system must give the lowest price charged for the SKU in that market in the previous 30 days, because Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Article 6a) requires an announced reduction to show it, which needs an effective-dated price history. Matches expected.

The reader names arrangement 4: consumer prices and the campaign calendar in the shop platform, wholesale and contract prices in the ERP, every other system fed by effective-dated price events and compared daily; quotes the three assumptions (price lists per market and group with validity windows and a history, the ERP invoices wholesale, dated events compared daily); and says a pricing service is better when any assumption fails or with many markets, currencies, customer groups or storefronts. Matches expected.

No material unexplained term for the declared audience. (a) Every does_not_know term is given at or before first use: price list, base, customer-specific, contract and tiered price, quote (What a Price Is Made Of ¶2); price selection rule (¶3); moment of selection (¶5); engine vs copies (components table and How the Pieces Fit Together ¶2); tax-inclusive/exclusive (Tax ¶1); One Stop Shop (Tax ¶4); converted and fixed prices (Tax ¶5); the 30-day prior-price rule (EU rules ¶2); price parity, price control mechanisms, Buy Box (EU rules ¶4); repricer, price change event, cost floor (Pieces ¶4-¶7, floor also in the failure-pattern callout). 'Price-state events' in EU rules ¶5 come before the price event is defined in Pieces ¶4, but the sentence glosses them as the marketplace's verdicts (Buy Box lost, offer suppressed, parity warning), and events are known from Part I. (b) The terms reader's slowed-me items are all on the audience's already_knows list: EDI, iPaaS, B2B and API (glosses already given); Waypoint W5 (decisions W1-W8); the Giant's Boots and the Long Fuse (the sixteen failure-pattern names); syndicated field (syndication from product-information); idempotent and reconciliation (Part I); Noor Visser, Eva, her order and exchange, bol, Nijmegen/Munich (Kestrel & Pine's systems, people and order journey); scale-stage names, including 'Omnichannel stage' in the trade-offs table (the four scale stages); shop platform, connector (Part I usage and glosses). The remaining items (vendor names, Europe1 with an explaining clause, SAP KBA, NL/BE/DE, 'one-price-everywhere story') are minor and do not block understanding. The flow readers flagged many of the same terms; they explain them to a reader who has not read Part I and are recorded under flow_is_followable as non-material for this audience.
